The Vision Atlas studies human visual stimulation and the EMDR hexagon hypothesis. Computer vision for genomics studies algorithms for hyperspectral image analysis. These are separate research directions. The word “vision” does not make them the same project, method or evidence base.

Quantum Atlas uses OXTR DNA inputs in computational and quantum experiments. Its hexagonal atom arrangement and quantum-stability hypothesis are separate from the Vision Atlas EMDR tracking hypothesis and from the proposed computer vision algorithm.
Read the saved study phases in order: original qualification runs, completed classical genomic pilot, further local CPU checks, then the proposed next quantum test.

RESEARCH STIMULUS · NATURE, 2022
Fibonacci pulses kept quantum information stable for longer.

Laser pulses arranged in a Fibonacci pattern extended the stability of information stored in a quantum computer’s atoms. This finding motivates our investigation and future experiments with Fibonacci representations.

SCIENTIFIC REVIEW
Gemini 4 Argon
OXTR · STUDY 01
Study insights
Connection verification
Fibonacci pulses and longer-lived quantum information
DUMITRESCU ET AL. · NATURE 607, 463–467 · 2022
Laser pulses arranged in a Fibonacci pattern kept quantum information stable for longer in the atoms of a quantum computer.

These observations concerned the edge qubits of a ten-ion processor. The Fibonacci-driven information remained coherent for the full 5.5-second observation period. The 1.5-second comparison is specific to that experiment, not a universal qubit lifetime.
The authors attribute the protection to symmetries emerging from the pulse ordering. Their experiment did not test a hexagonal atom arrangement or M9 P24.
A stimulus for our investigation

Quantum Atlas investigates the hexagonal and triangular structures in Fibonacci’s modular representations across M1–M1001. We are exploring whether those relationships have measurable consequences in quantum systems, using Fibonacci, Phi Ratio, Alpha, Beta, Gamma and Epsilon. OXTR DNA supplies the first biological test inputs.

The geometric mechanism illustrated below is our working hypothesis. Odom’s construction and the honeycomb theorem establish mathematical relationships; a connection to quantum coherence remains to be tested.
Enable JavaScript to explore a question. Read the research references.

geometry_explanations.fibonacci: Successive Fibonacci ratios approach the Phi Ratio. This is an exact limiting relationship. It does not by itself specify a physical arrangement of atoms.
geometry_explanations.modular: M9 P24 means nine residue classes in a 24-step cycle. The Atlas places period positions on a circle; Gamma and Epsilon visit six equally spaced positions. M1–M1001 lets us compare modular representations. These are mathematical coordinates, not nine physical spatial dimensions.
geometry_explanations.odom: Odom’s construction gives MP/MN = φ exactly: M and N bisect two sides of an equilateral triangle, and the ray MN meets its circumcircle at P. A regular tetrahedron has equilateral faces, so this construction applies within each face.
geometry_explanations.honeycomb: Hales proved that regular hexagonal tiling minimizes boundary length when the plane is divided into equal-area cells. This is a geometric efficiency theorem; it does not establish quantum stability or minimum energy for every physical system.
geometry_explanations.quantum: Working hypothesis: does the hexagonal structure associated with these representations contribute to quantum coherence? A direct test varies pulse ordering and atom geometry independently, with matched controls and a coherence measurement. The Nature study supports Fibonacci-driven quantum effects; it does not establish this geometric mechanism.

classical.title: The calculation check passed.
classical.finding: Before using a quantum machine, we checked that the program calculates the six-atom experiment correctly. Independent calculations agreed within the recorded error limits.

insights.title: What counted as a pass?
insights.text: The simulation had to agree with a separate calculation of the same six atoms. The recorded numerical limit was 0.1 percentage points; the measured largest difference was about 0.006 percentage points.

insights.title: What this lets us do
insights.text: Use the checked program in the next prediction experiment. The test for that experiment is whether it finds known protein-binding regions more accurately.

simulation.title: CUDA-Q passed the calculation check.
simulation.finding: We used two short DNA samples near OXTR. For each sample, we prepared its numerical measurements in eight ways: ordinary measurements, Fibonacci numbers, Phi Ratio, Alpha, Beta, Gamma, Epsilon and a shuffled comparison. That made 16 CUDA-Q programs. The GPU results passed the calculation check. The DNA sequences themselves stayed unchanged.

insights.title: The goal of this first check
insights.text: Verify that CUDA-Q runs the intended six-atom experiment. A result outside the agreed error limits means we stop and fix the calculation before relying on it.

insights.title: What “calculated” means in the charts
insights.text: It is the predicted atom behaviour from a separate computer calculation with hardware noise left out. It is a comparison value, not a target for biological success.

insights.title: What happened with the sequences?
insights.text: The computer calculation predicted more excited-state readings for Gamma and Epsilon in both samples, and fewer for Alpha and Beta. The 100-shot GPU samples vary around those predictions.

insights.title: What earns a positive biological result?
insights.text: CTCF is one transcription factor, a protein that binds DNA. The completed classical pilot tested predictions against CTCF laboratory measurements. It found no clear gain from Fibonacci spacing and Phi Ratio. The next quantum test asks whether the atom readings improve those predictions, including M9 P24, beyond ordinary and shuffled inputs.

quantum.title: Aquila returned all 16 runs. Agreement with the calculation was mixed.
quantum.finding: The machine returned usable readings for every program. Alpha and Beta gave fewer excited-state readings in both samples, as the computer calculation predicted. Gamma and Epsilon gave more in sample 1 but fewer in sample 2.

insights.title: Was this the result we wanted?
insights.text: We wanted usable measurements from every program. We got them. We also wanted to see how closely the machine followed the calculation; that agreement was mixed.

insights.title: Does “fewer” mean better?
insights.text: No. It means fewer atoms were read in the excited state. “As predicted” means the calculation also said fewer. It does not mean better protein-binding prediction.

insights.title: What needs checking again?
insights.text: Repeat the same inputs with the run order mixed up. If the Gamma and Epsilon differences persist beyond measurement variation, investigate hardware effects and the program before interpreting them biologically.

insights.title: What is the next biological test?
insights.text: Astra has completed the first classical comparison against known CTCF-binding regions. Next, test whether the quantum readings add predictive value. Keep ordinary and shuffled controls: the shuffled version also produced a large atom response in this first batch.

classical.title: The Fibonacci representations change the response to the same OXTR DNA.
classical.finding: Holding the DNA window and six-atom model fixed, changing its mathematical representation changes the calculated quantum response. The effects differ between the two OXTR windows: the representations do not act as one interchangeable Fibonacci pattern.

receipt.backend: SciPy reference + CUDA-Q CPU + Wolfram Quantum Framework

details: Six atoms, full 64-state evolution, all 15 pair interactions. Same coordinates, pulses and interactions in the GPU and Aquila programs.
Two motif-rich 256-base OXTR windows were selected without occupancy labels. They qualify execution and are not an independent prediction test.
Native Fibonacci, Phi Ratio, Alpha, Beta, Gamma and Epsilon are compared with ordinary and shuffled inputs.
Gamma and Epsilon produce distinct simulated responses. At 100 shots, measurement uncertainty can be larger than that difference.

insights.title: What this tells us about the occupancy question
insights.text: We have generated distinct candidate features from OXTR DNA. This batch did not compare them with measured transcription-factor occupancy, so improved prediction has not yet been established.

insights.title: The contribution of this first experiment
insights.text: It identifies which representations alter the calculated response and tests whether a physical quantum processor reproduces those changes. Those are concrete properties to examine before interpreting a response as biological information.

simulation.title: Gamma and Epsilon increase the simulated response in both DNA windows.
simulation.finding: Among the six proposed representations, Gamma and Epsilon produce the largest increases over ordinary input in the ideal model. The GPU samples accompany that reference calculation below. A larger atom response is not a measure of better binding-site prediction.

receipt.backend: CUDA-Q compiled programs → qBraid NVIDIA GPU

details: The circles show simulated excitation probabilities, not protein binding probabilities. Every point includes 100-shot sampling uncertainty.
The acceptance check uses six binomial standard errors plus two counts; it is an execution check, not a predictive-performance result.
No classifier was trained in this qualification batch. OXTR occupancy evaluation remains a separate phase using held-out biological evidence.

insights.title: Native Fibonacci and Phi Ratio
insights.text: Native Fibonacci changes the ideal response by -2.2 and -0.0 percentage points in windows 1 and 2. Phi Ratio changes it by -2.8 and -0.2. Their effect is much smaller in the second window.

insights.title: Alpha and Beta
insights.text: Both reduce the ideal response in both windows: Alpha -1.6 and -2.5 percentage points; Beta -0.6 and -1.7. The individual M9 P24 paths generate different responses.

insights.title: Gamma and Epsilon
insights.text: Gamma increases the ideal response by +1.7 and +3.1 percentage points; Epsilon by +2.0 and +6.1. Their different path ordering remains visible even though they use the same six period positions.

insights.title: Why the shuffled control matters
insights.text: The shuffled representation increases the second-window response by 7.4 percentage points, more than any proposed Fibonacci representation. Response size alone cannot identify a specific Fibonacci benefit.

quantum.title: Aquila reproduces some changes—and reveals a mismatch for Gamma and Epsilon.
quantum.finding: Alpha and Beta reduce the observed response in both OXTR windows, matching the direction predicted by the model. Gamma and Epsilon increase it in the first window but decrease it in the second. The hardware therefore does not reproduce one consistent ordering of the representations across both DNA windows.
details: The average absolute difference covers all 21 observables in each of 16 programs. It is descriptive, not an occupancy-prediction score.
59 measurements began with at least one atom missing and are excluded from the conditional response. 0 measurements were reported as failed.
An atom absent at readout can indicate excitation or loss. The displayed 95% intervals cover sampling uncertainty and do not include every hardware error.
These completed measurements qualify the execution route. Whether the representations improve OXTR occupancy prediction remains an independent biological test.

All contrasts are exploratory descriptions. There is one hardware task per representation and window, run in a fixed order. Sampling uncertainty, drift and systematic errors limit causal or repeatability claims; multiple comparisons have not been used to declare a significant winner.

insights.title: Native Fibonacci and Phi Ratio
insights.text: Native Fibonacci changes the measured response by -3.8 and +1.3 percentage points in windows 1 and 2. Phi Ratio changes it by -1.4 and -0.7. These are observed differences from ordinary input, not changes in biological binding probability.

insights.title: Alpha and Beta
insights.text: Alpha changes the measured response by -5.2 and -3.0 percentage points; Beta by -1.3 and -1.9. Their downward direction matches the model in both windows. This small batch does not establish that the pattern repeats reliably.

insights.title: Gamma and Epsilon
insights.text: Gamma changes the measured response by +0.9 and -0.7 percentage points; Epsilon by +3.7 and -1.6. The second-window reversal shows that the ideal model does not fully describe these hardware measurements.

insights.title: The control and the OXTR question
insights.text: The shuffled control has the largest measured response in window 2 (+11.0 percentage points). We have measured representation-dependent responses, but have not established a Fibonacci-specific predictive benefit. Occupancy labels were not tested in this batch.

comparison.finding: The first experiment shows that Fibonacci, Phi Ratio and the four M9 P24 paths generate different calculated responses to OXTR DNA. Aquila reproduces some directional changes but not all; the shuffled control also generates a strong response. This gives us candidate quantum features and a concrete simulation–hardware mismatch to investigate. It does not yet answer whether those features improve transcription-factor occupancy prediction: no occupancy predictor or held-out biological test was run.

beta.endpoint_rule: Exclude endpoints, include wraparound; raw residues used for sums. Empty interiors sum to zero.

epsilon.status: Proposed geometric traversal; physical interpretation not assessed.

atlas.grids: Alpha/Gamma/Epsilon: 24 period positions; Beta: 9 residue positions

reference.selection: Ensembl OXTR gene body plus 10,000 bases on each genomic side
reference.scope: A defined locus window; distal regulatory elements outside it are not captured. Overlapping records may extend beyond its boundaries.
reference.direction: OXTR minus strand; descending genomic coordinates

template.geometry: Six sites on a regular hexagon; ring radius and nearest-neighbour separation 9 micrometres, with one vertex at north. Positions are fixed throughout each run.
template.input: A 24-slot vector of motif/spacing descriptors. Each encoding uses the same source features and identical normalization fitted on training data only.
template.encoding: Global detuning varies with the input; fixed nonzero drive permits noncommuting evolution. Canonical representation weights/order define registered alternatives. No local detuning access is assumed.
template.output: Six excitation probabilities and fifteen labelled pair probabilities at the final time; additional times require distinct tasks and a new frozen version.
template.model: H(t)/hbar = Omega(t)/2 sum_i X_i - Delta_x(t) sum_i n_i + sum_i<j C6/r_ij^6 n_i n_j
template.c6_source: Read and freeze Aquila device capabilities at compilation; never infer a molecular interaction from this Hamiltonian.
template.symmetry: Global driving of this symmetric array can produce redundant single-site and pair features. Measure effective feature rank on training data and retain the same symmetry treatment across all encodings; six atoms do not imply 21 independent features.

variants.label: Ordinary representation
variants.role: Same biological descriptors in their original genomic order.

variants.label: Native Fibonacci
variants.role: Predeclared distance features from native Fibonacci gaps, with the physical base-pair range fixed before labels are inspected.

variants.label: Phi Ratio
variants.role: Ratios of neighbouring motif gaps; retain physical gaps and distinguish native ratios from modular residues.

variants.label: Alpha · M9 P24
variants.role: Full canonical residue order; never equate 24 period positions with 24 hours or a universal 24-base spacing.

variants.label: Beta · M9 P24
variants.role: Canonical 4,8,7,5,1,2 cycle. Six-of-nine membership alone is a broad divisibility feature.

variants.label: Gamma · M9 P24
variants.role: Canonical two-triangle order encoded in time. Shared positions alone do not distinguish Epsilon.

variants.label: Epsilon · M9 P24
variants.role: Canonical seven-visit path, with the repeated closing point retained. A timed encoding must pass a distinguishability check.

variants.label: Matched shuffled representations
variants.role: Seeded controls preserve feature distributions, pulse duration, energy-scale bounds and input information.

evaluation.target: Presence of reproducible TF occupancy in a defined assay and cell context; no claim of exact contact bases, affinity or causal regulation.
evaluation.selection_rule: Choose one human GRCh38 TF assay with replicates, appropriate controls, adequate locus coverage and no dependence on Fibonacci fit. Record accession, factor, cell, QC and label rules before fitting.
inputs: Predefined Fibonacci, Phi Ratio and M9 P24 descriptors
not_inputs: Experimental occupancy labels or ChIP signal
Assay-specific labels used to choose encodings
evaluation.splits: Chromosome/block-separated training and validation, with chr3/OXTR withheld from all fitting. Keep overlapping windows and biological replicates together.
evaluation.primary_metric: Difference in average precision on the frozen independent test set, QRC versus the strongest validation-selected classical model on identical inputs.
controls: Classical nonlinear model with identical representation features
CUDA-Q simulated reservoir using the same physical program
Matched shuffled encoding and label-permutation checks
secondary: Calibration and precision at a fixed recall
Sensitivity to window origin, strand and measurement uncertainty
evaluation.success: Positive held-out improvement with a prespecified uncertainty interval; report inconclusive or negative results without selecting a favourable encoding after testing. No speedup or aromatic mechanism follows from classification alone.
evaluation.uncertainty: Bootstrap independent genomic blocks, keep repeat shots within their sample, report intervals. A locus with too few labels receives a ranking with uncertainty, not a predictive-performance claim.

execution.simulation_route: Compile a checked time-evolution circuit, validate locally, then use the existing qBraid GPU route for supported compiled programs. Native CUDA-Q dynamics is an alternative only after runtime capability checks.
execution.parity: Identical coordinates, C6, pulse schedule, basis/readout convention and observation times. Freeze the discretized AHS program before compiling the matched simulation.
execution.budget_rule: No dispatch until the complete task count, provider quotes and shared budget reservation are recorded and approved for the run. Existing one-task approval is not reused.
execution.task_formula: number of frozen input windows × encoding variants × readout times × hardware repeats

cache.rule: Show cache provenance and run date. A replay of saved results never creates a new hardware receipt. A changed input or model invalidates its dependent result.

review.next: Evaluate the prespecified prediction benchmark against held-out biological observations.

qualification.scope: Execution and numerical qualification; no biological prediction result.

papers.scope: Selected primary research for a proposed Universal Informatics Quantum Lab guide. This is a focused selection, not a systematic review. Bibliographic records, original summaries and links only; no third-party figures or article text copied.

papers.title: Large-scale quantum reservoir learning with an analog quantum computer
papers.evidence: Preprint; Aquila quantum hardware and classical comparisons
papers.finding: Biological or other input features can be encoded into neutral-atom dynamics; measured observables feed a classical predictor. Experiments include classification and time-series tasks up to 108 qubits.
papers.limit: Performance is task-dependent. Synthetic kernel comparisons do not establish a general biological advantage or an OXTR result.

papers.title: Harnessing a 256-qubit Neutral Atom Simulator for Graph Classification
papers.evidence: Preprint; Aquila hardware on protein graphs
papers.finding: Measured Aquila responses supplied a quantum kernel for protein graph classification, with performance comparable to the selected classical graph benchmark.
papers.limit: Graph embedding restricts the tested subset. The study does not test OXTR, Fibonacci representations or transcription-factor occupancy.

papers.title: Quantum Reservoir Computing with Neutral Atoms on a Small, Complex, Medical Dataset
papers.finding: The authors used Aquila responses to generate features for medical-data classification and compared them with emulated features.
papers.limit: Emulated features showed overfitting. Aggregated feature selection risks test leakage in hardware comparisons; definitive hardware advantage over classical models remains unestablished.

papers.title: Quantum annealing versus classical machine learning applied to a simplified computational biology problem
papers.authors_short: Richard Y. Li, Rosa Di Felice, Remo Rohs and Daniel A. Lidar
papers.evidence: Peer reviewed; quantum hardware and classical comparisons
papers.finding: A D-Wave annealer classified and ranked experimental transcription-factor binding data using simplified small datasets.
papers.limit: Results depend on small training sets and the tested formulations; performance relative to classical methods declines as training data increase. This does not establish general quantum speedup.
papers.platform_relevance: A bridge to our DNA-binding research, with a classical baseline and held-out evaluation. It is not evidence for an OXTR-specific quantum result.

papers.title: Genome assembly using quantum and quantum-inspired annealing
papers.evidence: Peer reviewed; QPU, hybrid and classical quantum-inspired methods
papers.finding: DNA read ordering is expressed as a binary optimization problem and tested with synthetic sequences and bacteriophage-derived data.
papers.limit: The larger bacteriophage graph required manual classical partitioning and a hybrid backend; synthetic reads excluded sequencing errors. The work does not establish general superiority over classical assembly.
papers.platform_relevance: A small, inspectable read-ordering exercise can teach the path from DNA to graph to optimization to reconstructed sequence.

papers.title: Haplotype-resolved assembly of diploid and polyploid genomes using quantum computing
papers.evidence: Peer reviewed; small QPU proof of concept and separate classical scaling
papers.finding: The authors mapped phasing and assembly to a vehicle-routing formulation and reconstructed short synthetic diploid and triploid examples on D-Wave.
papers.limit: The larger human MHC-region experiment used Google's classical OR-Tools. The quantum examples used 50-base-pair diploid and 35-base-pair triploid sequences; these are not whole-genome QPU assemblies.
papers.platform_relevance: Teach both the optimization formulation and the boundary between a quantum demonstration and classical scaling.
papers.source_checked: Full article on PMC plus PubMed bibliographic record
papers.rights_note: Article is CC BY-NC-ND; retain our original summary and citation rather than reusing its figures.

papers.title: Quantum optimization of maximum independent set using Rydberg atom arrays
papers.finding: Rydberg arrays with up to 289 qubits experimentally solved maximum-independent-set graph instances.
papers.limit: This is a graph-optimization foundation, not a genomics experiment. The speedup comparison in the paper is scoped to its instances and classical simulated-annealing benchmark, not all classical solvers. It is not a record of execution on our Aquila account.
papers.platform_relevance: Explain why selecting mutually compatible graph vertices maps naturally to Rydberg blockade.
papers.source_checked: Author-hosted paper, arXiv record and MIT publication page

papers.title: A Scalable Heuristic for Molecular Docking on Neutral-Atom Quantum Processors
papers.authors_short: Mathieu Garrigues, Victor Onofre, Wesley Coelho and S. Acheche
papers.finding: A decomposed graph-based method was evaluated on ten protein-ligand complexes with 225–585 vertices.
papers.limit: The reported solver uses an emulator. This is not a QuEra Aquila hardware result, a general docking speedup, or demonstrated drug-discovery success. A greedy baseline is not the full range of classical docking methods.
papers.platform_relevance: An emerging docking direction, clearly labelled as simulation research alongside the hardware foundations.
papers.source_checked: arXiv v2 abstract and full HTML; no journal publication shown in the checked record

follow_through.question: Do regular Fibonacci sequences, M9 P24 including Alpha, Beta, Gamma and Epsilon, and Phi Ratio help predict transcription factor binding around OXTR?

cohort.sampling: 32 peak-centred and 32 nearby non-peak windows per development chromosome; all 152 fixed OXTR windows for evaluation. Non-peak means no peak reported in this assay, not proven absence.
cohort.model_selection: Use chr1 for learning, chr2 to choose a fixed candidate, then evaluate chr3/OXTR once. No OXTR labels enter fitting or candidate selection.
cohort.primary_measure: Average precision: how often regions ranked as likely binding regions match the laboratory peak map.
limits: Small pilot with five OXTR peak regions; descriptive results, not an independent confirmation.
Local background selection and one cell context limit generalisation.
No accessibility-matched negative set or ENCODE blacklist filtering in this pilot.
Additional hardware and population-wide inference are outside this task.

interpretation.answer: There is no demonstrated benefit yet for predicting binding around OXTR. Adding Fibonacci and Phi Ratio features gave an inconclusive result. The new classical test did not evaluate biological prediction by M9 P24 Alpha, Beta, Gamma or Epsilon. This pilot concerns CTCF, one DNA-binding protein measured in one stem-cell context, not transcription factors generally.
interpretation.what_we_did: The agent completed a comparison of ordinary DNA binding-pattern and spacing features, with and without Fibonacci/Phi Ratio features. It learned on chromosome 1, chose the method on chromosome 2 and tested OXTR on chromosome 3, without seeing OXTR laboratory answers during learning or selection. The agent also prepared a new matched pair of DNA windows: one overlapping a reported CTCF peak and one comparison window. For each, it compiled the same DNA eight ways—ordinary, Fibonacci, Phi Ratio, Alpha, Beta, Gamma, Epsilon and shuffled controls—and completed 16 local CUDA-Q CPU checks.
interpretation.meaning: At OXTR, average precision rose from 0.0719 to 0.0739. This is a ranking score, not percent accuracy. The uncertainty range for the change extended from −0.0263 to +0.0082, leaving benefit unresolved; the noisy increase establishes no advantage. The pilot covered only five OXTR peak regions and used laboratory data with quality warnings. Saved CUDA-Q/Aquila readings describe programmed atom excitation, not binding probabilities; the two saved samples overlap none of those peaks, so they do not validate binding prediction. The new matched pair checks programs, not predictive performance.
interpretation.next_dependency: A larger quantum prediction test still needs more matched quantum measurements linked to laboratory binding results, and a larger independent biological test remains necessary. Today’s instruction prohibits new Aquila submissions; none were made, and no new quantum jobs were submitted. Fresh device validation and explicit allowance are required before Aquila submission; new paid qBraid work also lacks a credit allowance. This is an automated preliminary report, with Gemini oversight deferred. The inconclusive result usefully separates completed program checks from evidence of predictive benefit.

field_guide.coordinate_system: GRCh38, zero-based start, end exclusive; each DNA window has 256 bases.
field_guide.reported_CTCF_peak: 1 means overlap with an ENCODE CTCF peak in GM23338 iPSCs; 0 means no reported peak, not proven absence.
field_guide.ordinary_score: Uncalibrated classifier ranking score, not measured binding probability.
field_guide.Fibonacci_Phi_score: Ranking from classical motif/spacing plus Fibonacci and Phi Ratio features, not a quantum prediction.
field_guide.average_precision: Area under the precision-recall step curve; rank measure, not percentage accuracy.
field_guide.block_bootstrap_95_interval: Descriptive interval from 1,000 genomic block resamples, excluding samples containing only one class.
field_guide.cudaq_observables: Six excitation probabilities followed by fifteen pair excitation probabilities. New local CPU simulation; not cloud GPU or QPU measurements.

classical.positive_result_rule: The added features improve average precision and the block-resampled interval remains above zero. This small pilot still needs a fresh independent dataset.
classical.negative_result_rule: An interval below zero is discouraging for this recipe; an interval spanning zero leaves benefit unresolved.
